content: Nebulin-related-anchoring protein (N-RAP) is a protein encoded by the NRAP gene in humans. It is a muscle-specific isoform that belongs to the nebulin family of proteins, which includes five members: N-RAP, nebulin, nebulette, LASP-1, and LASP-2. N-RAP plays a dual role in muscle biology, being involved in the formation of myofibrils during muscle development and in maintaining cell-cell connections in mature muscle tissue. N-RAP is a large protein with a molecular weight of 197 kDa, consisting of 1,730 amino acids. As a member of the nebulin protein family, it contains characteristic 35-amino-acid-long nebulin repeats, which serve as actin-binding domains. These repeats include a conserved SDxxYK motif. Additionally, groups of seven nebulin repeats form super repeats, which feature a conserved WLKGIGW motif at the end of the third repeat. A distinguishing feature of N-RAP, compared to nebulin, is its N-terminal cysteine-rich LIM domain, a structural element it shares with LASP-1 and LASP-2. N-RAP plays a critical role in the organization of myofibrils during the development of cardiomyocytes. It has been demonstrated that N-RAP is essential for the proper α-actinin-dependent assembly of myofibrils in embryonic cardiomyocytes. When N-RAP protein levels are reduced, myofibrillar disassembly occurs in these cells. Research suggests that the super repeats of N-RAP act as a scaffold for organizing α-actinin and actin into sarcomeric I-Z-I complexes in premyofibrils. Dynamic imaging studies have shown that N-RAP dissociates from these I-Z-I complexes once the assembly of actin thin filaments is complete. In adult cardiac muscle, N-RAP is localized to intercalated discs, where it anchors terminal actin filaments to the sarcolemma. It is thought that in mature muscle, N-RAP contributes to the transmission of force from the sarcomere to the extracellular matrix. Although no direct association has been identified between mutations in the NRAP gene and human cardiomyopathies, N-RAP expression is significantly upregulated in murine models of dilated cardiomyopathy. This upregulation is hypothesized to be an adaptive response aimed at compensating for the disorganized architecture of actin thin filaments at intercalated disc junctions in cardiomyocytes during the progression of dilated cardiomyopathy.
